{{redirect|Serre's criterion|the condition for a scheme to be affine|Serre's theorem on affineness}}
In [[commutative algebra]], '''Serre's criterion for normality''', introduced by [[Jean-Pierre Serre]], gives necessary and sufficient conditions for a commutative [[Noetherian ring]] ''A'' to be a [[normal ring]]. The criterion involves the following two conditions for ''A'':
*<math>R_k: A_{\mathfrak{p}}</math> is a [[regular local ring]] for any prime ideal <math>\mathfrak{p}</math> of height ≤ ''k''.
*<math>S_k: \operatorname{depth} A_{\mathfrak{p}} \ge \inf \{k, \operatorname{ht}(\mathfrak{p}) \}</math> for any prime ideal <math>\mathfrak{p}</math>.<ref>{{harvnb|Grothendieck|Dieudonné|1961|loc=§ 5.7.}}</ref>
The statement is:
*''A'' is a [[reduced ring]] <math>\Leftrightarrow R_0, S_1</math> hold.
*''A'' is a normal ring <math>\Leftrightarrow R_1, S_2</math> hold.
*''A'' is a [[Cohen–Macaulay ring]] <math>\Leftrightarrow S_k</math> hold for all ''k''.
Items 1, 3 trivially follow from the definitions. Item 2 is much deeper.

For an [[integral domain]], the criterion is due to [[Wolfgang Krull|Krull]]. The general case is due to Serre.

== Proof ==

===Sufficiency===
(After EGA IV<sub>2</sub>. Theorem 5.8.6.)

Suppose ''A'' satisfies ''S''<sub>2</sub> and ''R''<sub>1</sub>. Then ''A'' in particular satisfies ''S''<sub>1</sub> and ''R''<sub>0</sub>; hence, it is reduced. If <math>\mathfrak{p}_i, \, 1 \le i \le r</math> are the minimal prime ideals of ''A'', then the [[total ring of fractions]] ''K'' of ''A'' is the direct product of the residue fields <math>\kappa(\mathfrak{p}_i) = Q(A/\mathfrak{p}_i)</math>: see [[total ring of fractions#Total ring of fractions of a reduced ring|total ring of fractions of a reduced ring]]. That means we can write <math>1 = e_1 + \dots + e_r</math> where <math>e_i</math> are idempotents in <math>\kappa(\mathfrak{p}_i)</math> and such that <math>e_i e_j = 0, \, i \ne j</math>. Now, if ''A'' is integrally closed in ''K'', then each <math>e_i</math> is integral over ''A'' and so is in ''A''; consequently, ''A'' is a direct product of integrally closed domains ''Ae''<sub>''i''</sub>'s and we are done. Thus, it is enough to show that ''A'' is integrally closed in ''K''.

For this end, suppose
:<math>(f/g)^n + a_1 (f/g)^{n-1} + \dots + a_n = 0</math>
where all ''f'', ''g'', ''a''<sub>''i''</sub>'s are in ''A'' and ''g'' is moreover a non-zerodivisor. We want to show:
:<math>f \in gA</math>.
Now, the condition ''S''<sub>2</sub> says that <math>gA</math> is [[unmixed theorem|unmixed]] of height one; i.e., each [[associated prime]]s <math>\mathfrak{p}</math> of <math>A/gA</math> has height one. This is because if <math>\mathfrak{p}</math> has height greater than one, then <math>\mathfrak{p}</math> would contain a non [[zero divisor]] in <math>A/gA</math>. However, <math>\mathfrak{p}</math> is associated to the zero ideal in <math>A/gA</math> so it can only contain zero divisors, see [https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/3630663/zero-divisors-and-associated-primes-of-the-zero-ideal-in-a-noetherian-ring here]. By the condition ''R''<sub>1</sub>, the localization <math>A_{\mathfrak{p}}</math> is integrally closed and so <math>\phi(f) \in \phi(g)A_{\mathfrak{p}}</math>, where <math>\phi: A \to A_{\mathfrak{p}}</math> is the localization map, since the [[integral element|integral equation]] persists after localization. If <math>gA = \cap_i \mathfrak{q}_i</math> is the [[primary decomposition]], then, for any ''i'', the radical of <math>\mathfrak{q}_i</math> is an associated prime <math>\mathfrak{p}</math> of <math>A/gA</math> and so <math>f \in \phi^{-1}(\mathfrak{q}_i A_{\mathfrak{p}}) = \mathfrak{q}_i</math>; the equality here is because <math>\mathfrak{q}_i</math> is a <math>\mathfrak{p}</math>-[[primary ideal]]. Hence, the assertion holds.

===Necessity===
Suppose ''A'' is a [[normal ring]]. For ''S''<sub>2</sub>, let <math>\mathfrak{p}</math> be an associated prime of <math>A/fA</math> for a non-zerodivisor ''f''; we need to show it has height one. Replacing ''A'' by a localization, we can assume ''A'' is a local ring with maximal ideal <math>\mathfrak{p}</math>. By definition, there is an element ''g'' in ''A'' such that <math>\mathfrak{p} = \{ x \in A | xg \equiv 0 \text{ mod }fA \}</math> and <math>g \not\in fA</math>. Put ''y'' = ''g''/''f'' in the total ring of fractions. If <math>y \mathfrak{p} \subset \mathfrak{p}</math>, then <math>\mathfrak{p}</math> is a faithful <math>A[y]</math>-module and is a finitely generated ''A''-module; consequently, <math>y</math> is integral over ''A'' and thus in ''A'', a contradiction. Hence, <math>y \mathfrak{p} = A</math> or <math>\mathfrak{p} = f/g A</math>, which implies <math>\mathfrak{p}</math> has height one ([[Krull's principal ideal theorem]]).

For ''R''<sub>1</sub>, we argue in the same way: let <math>\mathfrak{p}</math> be a [[prime ideal]] of height one. Localizing at <math>\mathfrak{p}</math> we assume <math>\mathfrak{p}</math> is a [[maximal ideal]] and the similar argument as above shows that <math>\mathfrak{p}</math> is in fact principal. Thus, ''A'' is a regular local ring. <math>\square</math>
